claim: The scientific investigation of consciousness divides into two major branches: the study of 'state of consciousness' and the study of 'access to consciousness'.
source: The scientific investigation of consciousness divides into two major branches (Koch, 2004; Dehaene et al., 2014). The first branch, which studies the 'state of consciousness', focuses on general vigilance or a person's ability to perceive, interact, and communicate with the environment, by examining the regulation of sleep and waking, and their pathological disruption by coma, epilepsy, and sleep disorders (Laureys et al., 2004). The second branch of inquiry, which studies 'access to consciousness', focuses on the processes that make a specific content subjectively experienced—what differences in brain activity distinguish conscious vs unattended or subliminal stimuli (Dehaene et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Koch, 2004; Dehaene et al., 2014; Laureys et al., 2004; Dehaene et al., 2006) that establish this division in consciousness research.

claim: Paradigms comparing seen and unseen trials have yielded convergent findings about neural correlates of consciousness.
source: Such paradigms have yielded convergent findings (Koch, 2004; Dehaene and Changeux, 2011; Dehaene et al., 2014), but they have also been criticized on several grounds (Aru et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research (Koch, 2004; Dehaene and Changeux, 2011; Dehaene et al., 2014) that have used these paradigms.

claim: Differences in neural activity between seen and unseen trials may stem from physical differences in the stimuli.
source: First, differences in neural activity may stem from physical differences in the stimuli.
evidence: This is a known confound in consciousness research, based on established methodological knowledge in the field.

claim: Performance is typically much higher for conscious trials compared to unconscious trials.
source: Even then, stimuli also differ in their depth of processing: performance is typically much higher for conscious trials (Lau and Passingham, 2006), and several operations may only be feasible in the conscious state (Sackur and Dehaene, 2009; De Lange et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Lau and Passingham, 2006; Sackur and Dehaene, 2009; De Lange et al., 2011).

claim: The late P3 component of event-related potentials is a frequent signature of conscious perception.
source: For instance, the late P3 component of event-related potentials, which is a frequent signature of conscious perception (Dehaene and Changeux, 2011), has been proposed to reflect either a non-specific alerting effect arising from noradrenergic neurons of the locus coeruleus (Nieuwenhuis et al., 2005) or the activation of generic reporting processes unnecessary to conscious perception itself (Pitts et al., 2012, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior research (Dehaene and Changeux, 2011).

claim: The Global Neuronal Workspace (GNW) model asserts that when a stimulus gains access to consciousness, stimulus-specific information is amplified and re-encoded in additional areas, including a prefrontal–parietal network.
source: The Global Neuronal Workspace (GNW) model asserts that perceptual stages may unfold identically on conscious and non-conscious trials, but that, when a stimulus gains access to consciousness, stimulus-specific information is amplified and re-encoded in additional areas, including a prefrontal–parietal network.
evidence: This is a description of a theoretical model from the literature, representing established theoretical knowledge.

claim: Multiple macroscopic retinotopic maps are present throughout the human brain, including the frontal lobe.
source: We chose visual location as the decoded parameter of the stimulus, because multiple macroscopic retinotopic maps are present throughout the human brain, including the frontal lobe (Sereno et al., 1995; Hagler and Sereno, 2006), and therefore, the full cortical processing stream of this parameter should be more easily decodable than other more microscopic parameters, such as object identity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research (Sereno et al., 1995; Hagler and Sereno, 2006).

claim: There is an early stage (~100–200 ms) where location information was essentially confined to occipital, ventral visual, and lateral and mesial parietal regions.

evidence: This is a direct report of source localization analysis results, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

Above-chance classification could be achieved in all regions, including superior parietal, rostral middle frontal, and superior frontal regions, supporting the prior finding that these regions contain retinotopic maps (Sereno et al., 1995; Hagler and Sereno, 2006).

claim: The high level of decoding observed on seen trials, over a long time window of ~270–800 ms, combined with a low level of off-diagonal temporal generalization beyond a fixed horizon of ~160 ms, implies that a conscious location is successively encoded by a series of about four distinct stages, each terminating relatively sharply after a processing duration of ~160 ms.

evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal generalization results.

claim: The square pattern of the temporal generalization matrix on unseen trials suggests that unconscious information lingers in a single representational state, which decays slowly over time.
source: The square pattern of the temporal generalization matrix on unseen trials (Figure 5A) suggests that unconscious information lingers in a single representational state, which decays slowly over time, thus yielding a paradoxically longer endurance than on seen trials in the forward direction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal generalization results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Conscious access can be described as the entry of information into a dynamic routing system in which information is stabilized, transferred to a processor, exploited in a determined time, and then transferred again to the next stage.
source: They suggest that conscious access can be described as the entry of information into a dynamic routing system (Sackur and Dehaene, 2009; Dehaene et al., 2014) in which information is stabilized, transferred to a processor, exploited in a determined time, and then transferred again to the next stage.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of theoretical models, supported by citations (Sackur and Dehaene, 2009; Dehaene et al., 2014).

claim: A failure to attain a threshold-level activation at one of the processing stages cuts the process short, prevents the attainment of a conscious-level representation, and causes the information to linger and decay.
source: As described in accumulation-of-evidence models of decision making (Shadlen and Kiani, 2011), a failure to attain a threshold-level activation at one of these stages cuts the process short, prevents the attainment of a conscious-level representation, and causes the information to linger and decay.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of theoretical models, supported by citation (Shadlen and Kiani, 2011).

claim: The location of a briefly flashed stimulus can be accurately decoded from MEG and EEG signals for up to 800 ms, whether or not the stimulus is seen.
source: The results revealed that (1) the location of a briefly flashed stimulus can be accurately decoded from MEG and EEG signals for up to 800 ms, whether or not the stimulus is seen.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding from the decoding analyses.

claim: Seen and unseen stimuli are initially encoded identically, but after ~270 ms, the information is selectively amplified on 'seen' trials.
source: (2) Seen and unseen stimuli are initially encoded identically, but after ∼270 ms, the information is selectively amplified on 'seen' trials.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding from the decoding analyses.

claim: This observation replicates and extends earlier observations with seen and unseen words, digits and pictures during masking, and the attentional blink.
source: This observation replicates and extends earlier observations with seen and unseen words, digits and pictures during masking (Del Cul et al., 2007; Fisch et al., 2009), and the attentional blink (Sergent et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to prior research, supported by citations (Del Cul et al., 2007; Fisch et al., 2009; Sergent et al., 2005).

claim: Asymmetrical generalization indicates that shared spatial codes are active on unconscious and conscious trials, but that conscious trials also contain additional neural codes for stimulus location that are absent or weaker on unconscious trials.
source: (3) Asymmetrical generalization indicates that shared spatial codes are active on unconscious and conscious trials, but that conscious trials also contain additional neural codes for stimulus location that are absent or weaker on unconscious trials.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding from the cross-condition generalization analyses.

claim: Source localization traces conscious codes to superior parietal and superior frontal cortex.
source: Source localization traces those conscious codes to superior parietal and superior frontal cortex.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding from the source localization analyses.

claim: The dynamics of cortical coding differs on seen and unseen trials: conscious information undergoes a series of representational transformations, such that each decoder fails to generalize beyond ~160 ms, while unconscious information, although weaker, generalizes over a longer period.
source: (4) The dynamics of cortical coding, as revealed by temporal generalization matrices (King and Dehaene, 2014), also differs on seen and unseen trials: conscious information undergoes a series of representational transformations, such that each decoder fails to generalize beyond ∼160 ms, while unconscious information, although weaker, generalizes over a longer period.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding from the temporal generalization analyses, supported by citation (King and Dehaene, 2014).

claim: Only conscious stimuli can be passed through a series of discrete information-processing stages.
source: The latter finding fits with earlier observations that only conscious stimuli can be passed through a series of discrete information-processing stages (Sackur and Dehaene, 2009; De Lange et al., 2011; Charles et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to prior research, supported by citations (Sackur and Dehaene, 2009; De Lange et al., 2011; Charles et al., 2014).

claim: The observed characteristic peak-to-end duration of about 160 ms is compatible with the finding that conscious percepts tend to be locked to an ongoing theta (~4–7 Hz) or high delta (~1–3 Hz) rhythm.
source: The observed characteristic peak-to-end duration of about 160 ms is also compatible with the finding that conscious percepts tend to be locked to an ongoing theta (∼4–7 Hz) or high delta (∼1–3 Hz) rhythm (Melloni et al., 2007; Doesburg et al., 2009; Nakatani et al., 2014; Sitt et al., 2014), which is also the frequency range of slow positive event-related potentials, such as the P3.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the temporal dynamics findings to prior research on oscillatory activity, supported by citations (Melloni et al., 2007; Doesburg et al., 2009; Nakatani et al., 2014; Sitt et al., 2014).

claim: Perceptual switching in a binocular rivalry paradigm corresponds to the emergence of synchronized gamma rhythm embedded in theta envelope.
source: Doesburg et al. found that perceptual switching in a binocular rivalry paradigm corresponds to the emergence of synchronized gamma rhythm embedded in theta envelope (Doesburg et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research (Doesburg et al., 2009).

claim: In an attentional blink paradigm, the synchrony of fast oscillations (beta and gamma) with slow activity (theta and high delta) increased with practice, in parallel to improved stimulus visibility.
source: In an attentional blink paradigm, the synchrony of fast oscillations (beta and gamma) with slow activity (theta and high delta) increased with practice, in parallel to improved stimulus visibility (Nakatani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research (Nakatani et al., 2014).

claim: Theta activity was higher on visible trials compared to invisible trials in a masking paradigm.
source: Theta activity was also shown to be higher on visible trials compared to invisible trials in a masking paradigm (Melloni et al., 2007) and was successfully used to classify conscious vs vegetative patients (Sitt et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research (Melloni et al., 2007; Sitt et al., 2014).

claim: Conscious information is able to enter into a series of computational stages that are betrayed by a series of theta- or delta-like peaks.
source: It thus seems plausible that conscious information is able to enter into a series of computational stages that are betrayed by a series of theta- or delta-like peaks (Dehaene and Sigman, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results in the context of theoretical models, supported by citation (Dehaene and Sigman, 2012).

claim: Unconscious information fails to be sequentially dispatched to the successive steps of a serial task and, therefore, remains blocked within a fixed representational state, where it slowly decays.
source: Conversely, unconscious information fails to be sequentially dispatched to the successive steps of a serial task and, therefore, remains blocked within a fixed representational state, where it slowly decays.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal generalization results.

claim: Behavioral priming studies confirm that unconscious information lingers at detectable levels for hundreds of milliseconds or even seconds.
source: Behavioral priming studies confirm that unconscious information lingers at detectable levels for hundreds of milliseconds (Greenwald et al., 1996) or even seconds (Soto et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research (Greenwald et al., 1996; Soto et al., 2011).

claim: The results are incompatible with theories that postulate identical codes for conscious and unconscious information, which would only be distinguished by second-order metacognitive tags.
source: Our results are incompatible with theories that postulate identical codes for conscious and unconscious information, which would only be distinguished by second-order metacognitive tags (Lau and Passingham, 2006).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of theoretical models, with citation (Lau and Passingham, 2006).

claim: The results fit with theories that postulate that a conscious episode is distinguished by an amplification of incoming sensory information, possibly through reverberating loops, and its distributed representation in multiple distinct regions including parietal and prefrontal cortices.
source: They fit with theories that postulate that a conscious episode is distinguished by an amplification of incoming sensory information, possibly through reverberating loops (Lamme, 2006), and its distributed representation in multiple distinct regions including parietal and prefrontal cortices (Dehaene and Naccache, 2001; Dehaene et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of theoretical models, with citations (Lamme, 2006; Dehaene and Naccache, 2001; Dehaene et al., 2006).

claim: The results are highly convergent with intracranial local-field potentials and single-neuron recordings during binocular rivalry and continuous flash suppression.
source: These results are highly convergent with intracranial local-field potentials and single-neuron recordings during binocular rivalry and continuous flash suppression (Sheinberg and Logothetis, 1997; Kreiman et al., 2002; Panagiotaropoulos et al., 2012), which indicate that late neural discharges in higher cortical areas reflect which of two rivaling images are subjectively perceived.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the current findings to prior research, supported by citations (Sheinberg and Logothetis, 1997; Kreiman et al., 2002; Panagiotaropoulos et al., 2012).

claim: In the case of object identity, decodable neural activity is found in inferior and anterior temporal cortex but also in prefrontal cortex.
source: In the case of object identity, decodable neural activity is found in inferior and anterior temporal cortex (Sheinberg and Logothetis, 1997; Kreiman et al., 2002) but also in prefrontal cortex (Panagiotaropoulos et al., 2012) as reported here.
evidence: This is a citation to prior research (Sheinberg and Logothetis, 1997; Kreiman et al., 2002; Panagiotaropoulos et al., 2012).

claim: Prefrontal cortex appears at the confluence of conscious perception of object identity and location, making it a primary candidate for the integrated perception of a unified conscious scene or event.
source: Thus, this region appears at the confluence of conscious perception of object identity and location, making it a primary candidate for the integrated perception of a unified conscious scene or event (Oizumi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of theoretical models, with citation (Oizumi et al., 2014).

claim: Some recent experiments suggest that removing the need to report radically reduces the neurophysiological correlates of conscious perception, including the P3b component of event-related potentials, leaving only a posterior mid-latency component.
source: Some recent experiments suggest that removing the need to report radically reduces the neurophysiological correlates of conscious perception, including the P3b component of event-related potentials, leaving only a posterior mid-latency component (Pitts et al., 2012, 2014a, 2014b; Frässle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research (Pitts et al., 2012, 2014a, 2014b; Frässle et al., 2014).

claim: Many experiments involving a dual task are known to delay and dilute late ERPs and to distort conscious access.
source: However, many of those experiments involved a dual task, which is known to delay and dilute late ERPs (Sigman and Dehaene, 2008) and to distort conscious access (Marti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research (Sigman and Dehaene, 2008; Marti et al., 2010).

claim: In a 'passive attentive' auditory paradigm, late ERPs including the P3b component were found to contain decodable information about the conscious percept.
source: In such an auditory paradigm, late ERPs including the P3b component were again found to contain decodable information about the conscious percept (Wacongne et al., 2011; King et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research (Wacongne et al., 2011; King et al., 2013).

claim: A correlation of late neurophysiological activity with perceptibility was obtained in a variety of neurophysiological studies of human visual perception or rodent tactile perception.
source: A correlation of late neurophysiological activity with perceptibility was also obtained in a variety of neurophysiological studies of human visual perception (Quiroga et al., 2008; Kouider et al., 2013) or rodent tactile perception (Manita et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a citation to prior research (Quiroga et al., 2008; Kouider et al., 2013; Manita et al., 2015).

claim: The neurophysiological correlates of conscious perception uncovered here might be generalized to other experimental conditions.
source: With due caution, we, therefore, hypothesize that the neurophysiological correlates of conscious perception uncovered here might be generalized to other experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: 17 right-handed healthy adults (10 men, 19–30 years of age) with no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders participated in the study.
source: 17 right-handed healthy adults (10 men, 19–30 years of age) with no history of neurological or psychiatric disorders participated the study.
evidence: This is a direct report of participant demographics.

source: The data of 5 subjects were excluded due to failure in calibration, and these observers reported more than 85% of the target trials as seen (even with maximum masking contrast).

source: The intensity values to which subjects were calibrated ranged from 0 to 227, mean 131.46 (SE = 19.76).

source: The mask followed immediately and remained on the screen for 400 ms.

claim: A linear support vector machine (SVM) algorithm (with cost parameter C = 1) was employed for classification.
source: In all analyses, we employed a linear support vector machine (SVM) algorithm (with cost parameter C = 1) that was complemented with a continuous output method providing for each sample tested the probability of belonging to each of the possible classes (i.e., spatial locations) (Platt, 1999).
evidence: This is a direct description of the analysis method, with citation (Platt, 1999).

source: The data were randomly divided into 15 non-overlapping folds; the classifier was trained on fourteenfolds and tested on the one that was left out; this procedure was repeated 15 times for each time sample, so all fifteenfolds were eventually used for testing.
